title: Infection Principles in Skin Disease
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Skin is colonized from birth yet rarely infected, because a dry, acidic, constantly shedding surface and a resident flora adapted to it deny pathogens the steps they need. This chapter explains that defense, then follows what happens when it fails: how an organism enters, adheres, invades, and spreads, and why the depth it reaches names the disease. It separates damage caused by direct invasion from damage caused by toxins acting at a distance, and it ends with the host defects that invite specific organisms. Board questions usually give a lesion, a depth, or a host context and ask for the mechanism or the organism behind it.

connections.to: Bacterial, viral, and fungal skin pathogens (IN-12)
connections.how: This chapter supplies the general rules of entry, depth, and toxin action that the organism-by-organism chapter then applies.
Much of the redness, swelling, and tissue loss in a skin infection is the host inflammatory response, not the organism itself.
The pattern of skin infection identifies the arm of immunity that is missing, because neutrophils, T cells, and antibody each cover different organisms.
Staphylococcal exfoliative toxin and pemphigus foliaceus autoantibodies attack the same protein, desmoglein 1, and split skin at the same level.
Impaired lymphatic drainage and venous stasis leave protein rich interstitial fluid that clears bacteria poorly, which explains recurrent leg cellulitis.

terms.def: Microorganisms that live stably on normal skin and reproduce there without causing disease.
Organisms deposited on skin from the environment that do not establish long-term residence and are removed by washing and desquamation.
The slightly acidic film on the skin surface, pH about 4.5 to 5.5, produced by sweat, sebum breakdown, and keratinocyte metabolism.
Suppression of pathogens by resident flora that occupy attachment sites, consume nutrients, and release inhibitory products.

A small secreted peptide that damages microbial membranes; the cationic ones, such as beta-defensins and cathelicidin LL-37, are attracted to the anionic microbial surface, while sweat dermcidin is anionic and acts without that attraction.
A microbial surface molecule that binds a host structure, for example staphylococcal MSCRAMMs that bind fibronectin and collagen.
A secreted enzyme that opens a path through tissue, such as hyaluronidase degrading matrix, streptokinase dissolving the fibrin that would contain the organism, or DNase liquefying pus.
A staphylococcal serine protease (ETA, ETB) that cleaves the extracellular domain of desmoglein 1 and separates the upper epidermis.
A toxin that cross-links MHC class II to the T cell receptor variable beta region outside the peptide groove, activating T cells without antigen processing.
Separation of the epidermis under light lateral pressure on skin that looks intact, indicating loss of keratinocyte adhesion.
A necrotic ulcer with a black eschar and surrounding erythema, caused by bacterial invasion of dermal vessel walls, classically by Pseudomonas aeruginosa in neutropenia.
The specific break in the barrier, such as a fissure, bite, ulcer, catheter, or injection site, through which an organism reaches living tissue.

sections.title: Normal skin flora and how intact skin resists colonization

blocks.text: Normal skin carries a dense resident flora that does no harm on intact tissue, and most of these organisms are poorly equipped to invade. Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most abundant resident, a coagulase negative, catalase positive gram positive coccus that is harmless on the surface but forms biofilm readily, so it becomes a real pathogen once foreign material such as a catheter or prosthesis bypasses the barrier. Cutibacterium acnes, formerly called Propionibacterium acnes, is an anaerobic, lipophilic gram positive rod that lives deep in the pilosebaceous unit where oxygen is low and sebum is plentiful. Corynebacterium species, often called diphtheroids, favor moist intertriginous folds, and Malassezia yeasts are lipid dependent and therefore concentrate on sebaceous areas of the scalp, face, and upper trunk. Each organism occupies the niche its metabolism requires, which is why the site of a lesion is itself a clue to the organism.

Staphylococcus aureus is not a true resident of healthy skin, but about 20 to 30 percent of people carry it in the anterior nares at any time. This matters because the carrier's own nasal strain is the usual source of that person's later skin, soft tissue, and surgical site infection, and because carriage explains how an organism with real virulence factors stays close to a barrier it can exploit.

blocks.title: Resident flora and the niche each one requires
rows: Tolerates dryness and salt; forms biofilm
Needs moisture and higher pH of folds
Cannot make its own long chain fatty acids
blocks.caption: Flora distribution follows metabolic need, so site of disease predicts organism.

blocks.text: The defenses of intact skin work by denying a pathogen each step it needs. The stratum corneum is a mechanically tough, water poor sheet of corneocytes in a lipid matrix that few organisms can grow in or cross. The surface sits at pH about 4.5 to 5.5, which slows many pathogens, including S aureus, while the residents tolerate it. Sebum triglycerides are hydrolyzed by host and bacterial lipases into free fatty acids that inhibit many bacteria and dermatophytes, one reason tinea capitis is largely a childhood disease, before sebum output rises at puberty. Desquamation continuously sheds the outer corneocytes with whatever has attached to them. Keratinocytes add beta-defensins and cathelicidin LL-37, both strongly induced by injury and pattern recognition receptor signaling; being cationic, they are drawn to the anionic microbial membrane and disrupt it, while eccrine sweat contributes dermcidin, an unusual anionic peptide that is active without that electrostatic attraction. The resident flora then supply colonization resistance by occupying binding sites, consuming nutrients, and releasing inhibitory products.

blocks.title: Why colonization normally fails
steps: Organism lands on the surface
Dryness and tight corneocyte barrier limit growth
Acid mantle and sebum free fatty acids inhibit it further
Antimicrobial peptides disrupt its membrane
Resident flora occupy the remaining sites and nutrients
Desquamation sheds it before it establishes
blocks.caption: Each defense blocks a different requirement, so single defenses can fail without infection following.

blocks.title: Each defense and what removes it
rows: Cuts, bites, burns, fissures, eczema, maceration, catheters, injections
Alkaline soaps, occlusion, incontinence, chronic exudate
Prepubertal low sebum output, degreasing agents
Reduced expression in atopic dermatitis, which helps explain S aureus overgrowth there
Neutropenia, diabetes, T cell deficiency, immunosuppression
blocks.caption: Infection usually needs both a barrier break and a reason the next defense could not finish the job.

sections.title: Stages of a skin infection and what the depth reached tells you

blocks.text: A skin infection proceeds through a fixed sequence, and each step must be completed before the next becomes possible. Entry comes first: because intact stratum corneum excludes bacteria, nearly every bacterial skin infection begins at a break that exposes living tissue, such as a cut, bite, burn, fissure, chronic ulcer, follicular opening, or catheter. Adherence follows, mediated by adhesins binding matrix proteins exposed at the break: staphylococcal MSCRAMMs (microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules) bind fibronectin, collagen, and fibrinogen, while Streptococcus pyogenes uses protein F, lipoteichoic acid, and M protein, which also resists phagocytosis.

Colonization becomes invasion when the organism multiplies and secretes enzymes that open a path. Hyaluronidase degrades dermal hyaluronic acid, streptokinase and staphylokinase activate plasminogen and dissolve the fibrin the host lays down to contain the infection, DNase liquefies the DNA of dying neutrophils in pus, and streptolysins and staphylococcal alpha toxin lyse host cells outright. Spread then follows the path anatomy leaves open: superficial lymphatics, the loose subcutis, or the plane of the deep fascia, where blood supply is poor. Damage comes from two sources that are easy to conflate, microbial toxins and the host's own neutrophil proteases, reactive oxygen species, vascular leak, and microvascular thrombosis.

blocks.title: Stages of a bacterial skin infection
steps: Entry through a breach in the stratum corneum
Adherence by adhesins to fibronectin, collagen, or fibrinogen
Multiplication and local colonization
Invasion using hyaluronidase, kinases, and DNase
Spread along lymphatics, subcutis, or fascial plane
Damage from microbial toxins plus host inflammation
blocks.caption: Each stage must be completed, so interrupting any one of them prevents the disease.

blocks.text: Depth determines both appearance and severity. In the upper dermis and its superficial lymphatics, lymphatic anatomy contains the process, which produces a raised, sharply demarcated plaque; in the lower dermis and fat there is no such boundary, so the edge is flat and indistinct. Infection in the fascial plane destroys the perforating vessels and small nerves crossing it, which is why pain is out of proportion to the visible skin, the skin can become anesthetic, and spread is fast with little surface change at first.

S aureus; Pseudomonas after hot tubs
Whole follicle into dermis; carbuncle spans several
Raised, sharply demarcated plaque, early fever
S pyogenes (type II) or mixed aerobes and anaerobes (type I)
Pain out of proportion, anesthesia, crepitus with gas formers
blocks.caption: Border definition and systemic severity both track with depth.

blocks.title: Reasoning from border to level
blocks.text: A patient has a tender, bright red facial plaque whose edge you can trace with a fingertip, and fever began within hours. A sharp palpable border places the process in the upper dermis and its superficial lymphatics, which contain spread, so this is erysipelas and the organism is S pyogenes. Had the erythema faded into normal skin with no palpable edge, the level would be the lower dermis and fat, where no boundary exists, and S aureus would be plausible as well. Had the pain far exceeded the appearance with numb overlying skin, the level would be fascia.

blocks.predict: A diabetic patient with fissured interdigital tinea pedis develops erythema spreading up the leg with no palpable border. Which stage did the fungus supply, and what does the absent border say about depth?
blocks.explain: Name the stage, the level reached, and why the edge is indistinct.

sections.title: Invasion versus toxin: exfoliative toxins and superantigens

blocks.text: Skin disease from a bacterium follows one of two mechanisms, and separating them explains findings that otherwise look contradictory. In direct invasion the organism is in the lesion, so the lesion yields it on culture and damage concentrates where the bacteria are. In toxin mediated disease the organism may sit at a distant, trivial focus while its toxin travels in the blood, so the affected skin is sterile and widely involved.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is the clearest example of a toxin acting at a distance. Exfoliative toxins A and B are glutamate specific serine proteases that cleave the extracellular domain of desmoglein 1, the desmosomal cadherin holding keratinocytes together in the superficial epidermis. Cutting it splits the skin high, within the stratum granulosum, giving flaccid blisters, a positive Nikolsky sign, and sheets of peeling that heal without scarring because dermis and basal layer are untouched. Mucosa is spared because it relies chiefly on desmoglein 3. The focus is usually the nose, conjunctiva, or umbilicus, so blister fluid is sterile and culture must come from there. The toxin is cleared renally, so infants, whose clearance is immature and who lack protective antitoxin antibody, and adults with renal impairment reach damaging systemic levels. Bullous impetigo is the same toxin acting locally, so its lesions do contain organisms.

Superantigens damage skin by a different route: they do not injure keratinocytes at all, they hijack T cell activation. Staphylococcal TSST-1 and the streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins bind MHC class II and the variable region of the T cell receptor beta chain at once, outside the peptide binding groove. Antigen processing and peptide specificity are bypassed, so every T cell carrying a susceptible V beta family activates regardless of what it recognizes, up to roughly a fifth of the repertoire. The resulting flood of interleukin 2, tumor necrosis factor, and interferon gamma produces high fever (at or above 38.9 degrees Celsius, 102 degrees Fahrenheit), diffuse erythema resembling sunburn, capillary leak with shock, and later desquamation of palms and soles. Staphylococcal toxic shock often has no bacteremia and only a colonized focus, whereas streptococcal toxic shock accompanies invasive infection.

sections.title: Host predisposition and predicting the organism from context

blocks.text: Host factors are not vague risk; each removes a specific defense, and the defense that is gone predicts the organism. Diabetes mellitus removes three at once: neuropathy abolishes the pain that would have revealed a wound, vascular disease limits delivery of oxygen and leukocytes, and sustained hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and oxidative killing. The diabetic foot therefore carries a chronic ulcer colonized from skin and bowel flora, which is why established infection there is polymicrobial. Ketoacidosis adds a separate problem: acidosis releases iron from transferrin and Rhizopus possesses a ketone reductase, so mucormycosis clusters in that metabolic state.

Venous insufficiency and lymphedema act through drainage rather than killing. Protein rich fluid that is not cleared supports bacterial growth, and poor lymphatic flow delays delivery of organisms and antigen to regional nodes where a response would be mounted. Beta hemolytic streptococci thrive here, and each episode scars lymphatics further, so recurrence becomes self reinforcing. Tinea pedis matters because macerated interdigital fissures are a reliable portal for those same streptococci, which is why interdigital disease and recurrent leg cellulitis travel together. Injection drug use delivers surface and oral flora straight into dermis, subcutis, or vein, so S aureus including methicillin resistant strains dominates, and spore forming Clostridium species may follow contaminated material into devitalized tissue.

Immune cell defects give the most predictable patterns. Neutrophils are the main defense against pyogenic bacteria, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and molds, so neutropenic patients develop Pseudomonas and Aspergillus or Fusarium lesions, and because pus is largely neutrophils those lesions are necrotic rather than purulent. Ecthyma gangrenosum shows the mechanism directly: bacteria invade dermal vessel walls, thrombose them, and infarct the overlying skin into a black eschar. T cells control intracellular and chronic surface pathogens, so T cell deficiency from advanced HIV infection or transplant immunosuppression brings severe or disseminated herpes simplex and varicella zoster, persistent molluscum and warts, and mucocutaneous candidiasis, with the Th17 and interleukin 17 axis specifically responsible for keeping Candida off skin and mucosa.

blocks.title: The lymphedema and cellulitis cycle
steps: Impaired lymphatic drainage leaves protein rich fluid
Bacterial clearance and antigen delivery to nodes are delayed
Streptococcal cellulitis develops
Inflammation scars lymphatic channels further
Drainage worsens, so the next episode comes more easily
blocks.caption: Each episode increases susceptibility, which explains recurrence in the same limb.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology set the rules this chapter follows. The layered structure of skin and the position of lymphatics, loose subcutaneous tissue, and deep fascia decide how far an organism can spread and therefore what the lesion looks like, while the molecular biology of the desmosome explains why one toxin splits the epidermis high and spares mucosa. Microbiology supplies the virulence factors, immunology supplies the defenses and the two toxin mechanisms, and pathology supplies the final common pathway, since neutrophil proteases, vascular leak, and microvascular thrombosis cause much of the visible damage in both invasive and toxin mediated disease.

Reasoning on the exam runs in either direction. Given a lesion, work from depth and border to level, then to the organisms that reach that level. Given a host, work from the defense that is missing to the organisms it was holding back. Both chains have limits worth respecting: depth and appearance overlap in early disease, cultures of superficial lesions and ulcers are often contaminated with colonizers rather than the causative organism, carriage of an organism is not the same as infection by it, and an exposure history in a vignette frequently outweighs the host factors. Where two mechanisms could produce the same picture, the distinguishing evidence is usually the level of the split, whether the affected skin itself contains organisms, and whether mucosa is involved.

summary: Resident flora occupy niches set by their metabolism: S epidermidis across the surface, C acnes deep in sebaceous follicles, Corynebacterium in moist folds, Malassezia where sebum lipids are plentiful.

Intact skin resists colonization through dryness, an acid mantle of pH about 4.5 to 5.5, sebum derived free fatty acids, desquamation, antimicrobial peptides (beta-defensins, cathelicidin LL-37, dermcidin), and colonization resistance from the flora themselves.
S aureus is carried in the anterior nares by about 20 to 30 percent of people, and the carrier's own strain is the usual source of later skin and surgical site infection.

Infection proceeds through entry, adherence by adhesins to matrix proteins, invasion using hyaluronidase, kinases, and DNase, spread along tissue planes, then damage from both toxins and host inflammation.

Depth names the disease: epidermis in impetigo, follicle in folliculitis, upper dermis and lymphatics in erysipelas with a sharp raised border, lower dermis and fat in cellulitis with an indistinct edge, walled off pus in abscess, and fascia in necrotizing fasciitis.
Pain out of proportion to the skin, anesthesia, and rapid spread indicate fascial involvement, because perforating vessels and nerves are destroyed before the surface changes.
Exfoliative toxins A and B cleave desmoglein 1 in the stratum granulosum, producing sterile flaccid bullae with a positive Nikolsky sign and spared mucosa, since mucosa relies on desmoglein 3.
Scalded skin syndrome affects infants and adults with renal impairment because the toxin is cleared renally, and the staphylococcal focus is distant, so culture the focus rather than the blister.

Superantigens bridge MHC class II and the T cell receptor V beta region outside the peptide groove, activating up to about a fifth of T cells and producing cytokine driven fever, diffuse erythema, shock, and late palmar desquamation.

The missing defense predicts the organism: polymicrobial infection in the diabetic foot, group A streptococci with lymphedema or tinea fissures, S aureus with injection drug use, Pseudomonas and molds in neutropenia, and herpesviruses, molluscum, and Candida in T cell deficiency.

verify: Prevalence of S aureus nasal carriage is given as about 20 to 30 percent, the usual range in standard texts, although Jawetz quotes figures as high as 50 percent for intermittent carriage. Confirm the figure NABNE expects.
Surface skin pH is given as about 4.5 to 5.5, but ranges from 4.0 to 6.0 appear in different dermatology and microbiology sources, and the value varies by body site.
The fraction of T cells activated by a superantigen is commonly stated as up to about 20 percent, with some sources citing up to 30 percent. The chapter uses about one fifth.
Whether NABNE Part I expects the current genus name Cutibacterium acnes or the older Propionibacterium acnes; both are given here.
Whether the eponyms Nikolsky sign, ecthyma gangrenosum, erysipeloid, and the type I versus type II classification of necrotizing fasciitis are tested, or only the descriptive mechanisms.

The toxic shock case definition fever threshold is given as at or above 38.9 degrees Celsius (102 degrees Fahrenheit) from public health case definitions; confirm whether a numeric threshold is tested at all on Part I.
Whether exfoliative toxin D is expected in addition to ETA and ETB; only ETA and ETB are stated here, as they are the toxins consistently described in standard texts.
